Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/health/gut-microbiome-measuring-microbes-and-setting-standards-better-health Only about half of the cells in your body are human . The other half are trillions of microbes that thrive on or inside your body to form a group of biological communities known as the human microbiome. These microbial communities can vary greatly in size and character. The digestive tract hosts the largest number of microbes, forming a complex ecosystem known as the gut microbiome. Concentrated primarily in the large intestine, it consists of thousands of different species of bacteria, viruses, fungi and other microorganisms . Like a fingerprint, your gut microbiome is entirely unique. It starts developing the moment you are born. Over time, the amount and types of microorganisms change based on factors such as your environment and diet. We could not survive without these microscopic companions. Most share a symbiotic relationship with us, offering vital benefits while enjoying food and shelter in our body. They play such an active and critical role in maintaining our health that many scientists consider the gut microbiome to be an organ of its own . The microbes within the digestive tract help us get the most out of our diet. These gut microbiota break down complex carbohydrates such as starches and fibers that our bodies cannot digest alone. This process produces helpful compounds that can guard against obesity and diabetes . On top of that, these microbes supply the enzymes needed to synthesize essential vitamins, such as B1 and K. The gut microbiota train immune cells to distinguish them from dangerous pathogens, helping the body fend off toxins more effectively. By competing with invading microorganisms for space and nutrients, they prevent harmful bacteria from multiplying. The gut microbiome is believed to interact with many other systems in our body, such as the endocrine and nervous systems, through connections that researchers are still actively studying. Experts are only beginning to understand the relationships between the gut microbiome and different diseases. Because each of us is a unique, complex organism, these relationships are vastly challenging to untangle. Just because changes in the gut microbiome correlate with a particular disease doesn’t necessarily mean they cause it in an individual. Still, it’s clear that the signals gut microbes send to each other and to cells elsewhere in the body significantly affect our health. In the last decade, scientists have linked the gut microbiome to a raft of human diseases, from inflammatory bowel disease to autoimmune disorders and obesity. Two highly active areas of research are in neurological conditions and cancer treatments. Through the connection between the digestive tract and the central nervous system, known as the gut-brain axis, gut microbes are thought to affect mood and mental health, and perhaps influence outcomes for neurological conditions, such as Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers are also investigating the link between gut microbiota and cancer. There is a growing body of research examining the role that the gut microbiome plays in how well a person responds to certain cancer treatments. While much remains to be learned about the gut microbiome’s connection to cancer, scientists have an immense opportunity to improve human health if they can uncover the underlying mechanisms. The gut microbiome holds great potential in the treatment of diseases. There are already therapies that target the restoration of the gut microbiome. Probably the most well known is the therapy called fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). An FMT is exactly what it sounds like: the transfer of fecal material, typically from a healthy donor, to restore the gut microbiome. Transplantation is commonly carried out through a colonoscopy, though doctors can also deliver the transplant through other methods, such as a capsule the patient swallows or a feeding tube inserted through the nose (known as a nasoduodenal tube). FMTs are most commonly used to treat recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI), a sometimes-deadly bacterial infection commonly picked up in hospitals. The microorganisms from the transplant help regenerate the healthy ecosystem in the gut microbiome, assisting the immune system in fighting off the infection. For recurrent CDI , the procedure has a success rate of up to 90% , a remarkable result for just about any therapy.
